```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(CorOncoEndpoints)
ctl <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, death.prop = 0.15,
               os.median = 15, pps.hr.resp = 0.6)
trt <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6 / 0.7, orr = 0.45, resp.cor = 0.40,
               death.prop = 0.15, pps.hazard = ctl$gam0, pps.hr.resp = 0.6)
arms <- list(Control = ctl, Treatment = trt)
```

This vignette shows how the settings of a trial are specified: accrual,
dropout and the censoring of PFS, the observation of response, groups with two
of the three endpoints, and random-number streams for simulations run in
batches. Time is in months throughout.

## Accrual

Accrual is specified as in the FastSurvival package. `a.time` gives the
breakpoints of the accrual intervals, and the number of patients in each
interval is given by rates in patients per month (`a.rate`) or by proportions
(`a.prop`). The rates refer to all groups together. The number of patients of
each group in each interval is fixed, and the patients are placed uniformly
within their interval.

With one more rate than intervals, the last rate applies to an open final
interval that ends when all patients are enrolled. Below, 10 patients per month
are enrolled for 6 months and then 30 per month until the 300 patients are
enrolled.

```{r}
d1 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(150, 150), arms = arms,
                     a.time = c(0, 6), a.rate = c(10, 30), seed = 1)
table(interval = cut(d1$accrual_time, c(0, 6, Inf), right = FALSE), d1$group)
max(d1$accrual_time)
```

The first 6 months enroll `r 10 * 6` patients, `r 10 * 6 / 2` per group, and
accrual ends at month `r 6 + (300 - 10 * 6) / 30`. With as many rates as
intervals, the rates must accrue the total sample size; otherwise an error
suggests the alternatives. Proportions describe the same pattern without
rates:

```{r}
d2 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(150, 150), arms = arms,
                     a.time = c(0, 6, 14), a.prop = c(0.2, 0.8), seed = 2)
table(interval = cut(d2$accrual_time, c(0, 6, 14), right = FALSE), d2$group)
```

Accrual may start after time 0, for example for the patients of the expansion
of a trial. Here 20 patients per month are enrolled from month 12:

```{r}
d3 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(50, 50), arms = arms, a.time = 12,
                     a.rate = 20, seed = 3)
range(d3$accrual_time)
```

`ExpectedEvents()`, `AverageHR()` and `RequiredEvents()` take the same
arguments:

```{r}
ExpectedEvents(arms, n = c(150, 150), a.time = c(0, 6), a.rate = c(10, 30),
               endpoint = "os", time = c(12, 24, 36))
```

## Dropout and censoring of PFS

Dropout is exponential with hazard `d.hazard` (or median `d.median`) and
censors PFS and OS. A proportion `q` lost to follow-up within a year
corresponds to the hazard `-log(1 - q) / 12` per month. Piecewise exponential
dropout is given by hazards in `d.hazard` and breakpoints in `d.time`.

`pfs.cens.hazard` adds a censoring time that applies to PFS only, for example
the start of another anticancer therapy before progression, after which OS is
still followed. Both censoring mechanisms are independent of the endpoints.

```{r}
q <- 0.05
d4 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(2000, 2000), arms = arms, a.time = c(0, 12),
                     d.hazard = -log(1 - q) / 12, pfs.cens.hazard = 0.02, seed = 4)
c(dropout_within_a_year = mean(d4$dropout_time <= 12),
  pfs_censored_by_therapy = mean(d4$pfs_cens_time < pmin(d4$pfs_time, d4$dropout_time)),
  os_events = mean(d4$os_event))
d5 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(2000, 2000), arms = arms, a.time = c(0, 12),
                     d.hazard = c(0.02, 0.005), d.time = c(0, 12, Inf), seed = 5)
c(dropout_before_12 = mean(d5$dropout_time <= 12), expected = 1 - exp(-0.02 * 12))
```

## Observation of response

The column `response` of the generated data is the response of the patient,
whether or not it would be observed. `CutoffData()` decides which responses
are observed at an analysis. With `resp.timing = "landmark"`, the response is
determined at the first tumor assessment `resp.tau`, and it is observed only
if the patient is still followed then; with `resp.timing = "ttr"` the time to
response plays this role. In `response_obs`, a patient without an observed
response counts as a non-responder, as in an intention-to-treat analysis, and
`response_eval` indicates the patients who were followed up to the first
assessment, for an analysis restricted to them.

```{r}
lm_arm <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, death.prop = 0.15,
                  os.median = 15, resp.timing = "landmark", resp.tau = 1.5)
d6 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = 20000, arms = lm_arm, a.time = c(0, 12),
                     d.hazard = 0.05, seed = 6)
c6 <- CutoffData(d6, cutoff = 24)
c(response = mean(c6$response), observed_itt = mean(c6$response_obs),
  observed_among_assessed = mean(c6$response_obs[c6$response_eval == 1]))
```

Because dropout is independent of response, the proportion among the patients
who were assessed estimates the response rate of `r lm_arm$orr`, whereas the
intention-to-treat proportion is expected to be
`r lm_arm$orr` times the probability of being followed up to month
`r lm_arm$tau`, that is, `r round(lm_arm$orr * exp(-0.05 * lm_arm$tau), 3)`. The
input `orr` is therefore the response rate without dropout.

## Two of the three endpoints

A group can be described by two endpoints through `endpoints` in `OncoArm()`;
the columns of the third endpoint are then `NA`. With PFS and OS only, the
response inputs are not needed:

```{r}
po <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 15,
              endpoints = c("pfs", "os"))
CorEndpoints(po)
```

With OS and response only, OS is exponential and is linked to response
directly, so that `resp.cor` is the correlation between OS and response:

```{r}
osr <- OncoArm(os.median = 15, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.35,
               endpoints = c("os", "response"))
CorEndpoints(osr)
head(rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = 5, arms = osr, seed = 7)[
  , c("pfs_time", "os_time", "response")])
```

Alternatively, the three endpoints can be generated and PFS ignored. The
correlation between OS and response is then a result of the other inputs, here
`r round(CorEndpoints(ctl)[["cor.os.resp"]], 3)` for the control group, and OS
is not exponential.

## Correlation between PFS and OS as input

The proportion of PFS events that are deaths can be replaced by a target
correlation between PFS and OS:

```{r}
pc <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, pfs.os.cor = 0.55,
              os.median = 15)
c(death.prop = pc$death.prop, CorEndpoints(pc)["cor.pfs.os"])
```

The attainable correlations are limited by the medians: with medians of 6 and
15 months, values above about
`r round(CorEndpoints(OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, death.prop = 1e-4, os.median = 15, endpoints = c("pfs", "os")))[["cor.pfs.os"]], 2)`
cannot be reached, and `OncoArm()` then reports the attainable range.

## Simulations in batches

A large simulation can be run in batches with the same `seed` and different
values of `stream`. Each stream is an independent sequence of random numbers,
so a batch gives the same data whether the batches are run one after another
or in parallel.

```{r}
batch <- function(b) {
  rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 10, n = c(150, 150), arms = arms, a.time = c(0, 12),
                 seed = 2026, stream = b)
}
identical(batch(1), batch(1))
identical(batch(1)$pfs_time, batch(2)$pfs_time)
```
